1 police officer killed in explosion in northern Spain
text: MADRID, Nov. 10 (Xinhua) -- One police officer was killed and another injured in an explosion on Tuesday morning in Oviedo, northern Spain, Spanish news agency EFE reported, citing National Police sources.

The officers discovered a backpack containing an explosive device at a residential building in the city's Villafria neighborhood at around 7:00 a.m. local time (0600 GMT) while responding to a shooting incident that left a woman injured, and the device subsequently detonated, EFE reported.

Citing the Spanish National Police union Jupol, EFE said that the blast killed an officer from the police canine unit. The injured officer, a specialist from the National Police's bomb disposal unit, lost a leg and remains in serious condition.
National Police sources said officers are searching for the suspect in the shooting, who may still be armed.  ■

items.title: News Analysis: Military exercise highlights Europe's bid for role in Ukraine peace talks
text: WARSAW, Nov. 9 (Xinhua) -- As a new round of talks between Russia, the United States and Ukraine approaches, the Britain- and France-led Coalition of the Willing launched its first military exercise in Poland on Monday to prepare for a possible deployment to Ukraine after hostilities end.
The exercise comes as European officials press for a role in the negotiations and analysts say the coalition is seeking to demonstrate its military credibility.

Russia, however, criticized such a deployment, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova warning Saturday that any foreign military units deployed in Ukraine would be regarded as legitimate targets.
The exercise, code-named "KOALICJA 26.2," runs from Nov. 9 to 22 and involves about 2,800 military personnel from 11 countries, including Britain, France, Germany, Belgium, Spain and Poland.

According to the British Ministry of Defence, the exercise will test command-and-control arrangements, rehearse the movement of personnel, equipment and supplies, and assess how different units can operate together as a multinational force.
"This isn't a hypothetical plan, it's a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops," British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in a statement.

Directed from its operational headquarters in Paris, the multinational force has its land and air components around Nowa Deba in southeastern Poland, about 100 km from the Ukrainian border, while Turkish forces test arrangements for maritime mine clearance in Istanbul.
The drills are being held under the Coalition of the Willing, a group established in 2025 that comprises more than 30 countries, mostly European ones. The United States is not included.
Poland's Defense Ministry said the country hosts the main part of the exercise and provides logistical support, but did not plan to send troops to Ukraine after the conflict ends.
The exercise began a day before Russia, the United States and Ukraine were due to resume peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, amid disagreements over Europe's participation.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Monday that the European Union (EU) would be present while the Kremlin said the core negotiations would involve Russia, Ukraine and the United States. The exact format of European participation remained unclear.
Euronews reported Monday that concerns were growing in European capitals that decisions on the continent's security could be made without their involvement.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas stressed Friday the bloc's role in Europe's security architecture and the need to integrate Ukraine into it. She said any peace agreement would require the EU's involvement to be implemented.
French daily Le Monde said the exercise was intended to demonstrate the coalition's military credibility, with European countries hoping it would give them a say in discussions on Ukraine's future.

American's decades-long bond with Chinese hometown leaves legacy of kindness
text: XINING, Nov. 11 (Xinhua) -- In 1987, when David V. Plymire first returned to Huangyuan, the plateau county in China he had left decades earlier for the United States, locals were surprised that he still spoke the local dialect fluently.
"I simply talked to myself in front of a mirror so that I wouldn't forget the dialect of my hometown," he later explained to a local journalist.

Born in 1931 in the United States, Plymire spent his formative years with his family in Huangyuan County, now in northwest China's Qinghai Province, before leaving at age 18. Now, the 95-year-old regards the county as his only hometown.
Though an ocean away, Plymire never stopped thinking about the people of Huangyuan. Between 1987 and 2016, he returned more than 20 times, helping improve local health care and education.
To support the once-underdeveloped county, he donated over 30 pieces of medical equipment worth some 6 million yuan (about 895,500 U.S. dollars) to the Huangyuan County People's Hospital.

The donation included a CT scanner worth 350,000 U.S. dollars -- a piece of equipment that no other county-level hospital in Qinghai possessed at the time. The procurement and customs clearance process for the large machine was cumbersome, and only after numerous setbacks did it finally arrive in Huangyuan in 2000.
Standing before the device, Plymire bowed deeply. "This scanner must serve the people of my hometown well," he said in the local dialect.

In 2002, Jia Chengwu, a neurosurgeon from Shenyang, capital of northeast China's Liaoning Province, was dispatched to Huangyuan as part of the country's efforts to promote large-scale development of the western region. There, he performed the county's first craniotomy on a migrant worker with a head injury.

"Without the CT scanner donated by Mr. Plymire, which enabled a timely diagnosis of the worker's intracranial hematoma, I could not have completed that surgery," Jia recalled. "With this batch of donated hardware and the paired assistance from supporting doctors, the hospital became a well-known medical institution in the surrounding area."
Huang Jiong, head of the hospital, said the CT scanner remained in service for 15 years until around 2015, benefiting more than 20,000 people.

The equipment allowed doctors to quickly diagnose hundreds of critically ill patients suffering from cerebral hemorrhage, cerebral infarction and meningitis, securing precious time for surgical rescue and saving numerous lives, Huang said.
In addition to donating medical equipment, Plymire also coordinated with foreign friends to teach English at local schools.
His sister, Mary Ann Plymire, who was born and grew up in Huangyuan, funded the purchase of the county's first ambulance.
In 1998, the Huangyuan county government awarded both of them honorary citizenship.
At Mary's request, her ashes were brought back to the county after she died in 2016, allowing her to rest in peace in the place where she spent her childhood.
The roots of their devotion trace back to their father, Victor G. Plymire, a missionary who arrived in China in 1908 and settled in Huangyuan in 1921.

items.title: Chinese VP meets UN chief
text: ANTALYA, Türkiye, Nov. 11 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, as President Xi Jinping's special representative, met with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday on the sidelines of the Antalya Leaders' Summit at the 31st meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change.
Conveying Xi's cordial greetings to Guterres, Han said that China attaches great importance to climate change.

Last year, Xi announced China's 2035 Nationally Determined Contributions, and made it clear that China will "strive to do better," showing China's firm resolve and utmost efforts to address climate change.
This year, China set targets for non-fossil energy sources to account for 50 percent of power generation and electricity to account for 35 percent of final energy consumption by 2030, Han noted.

China is committed to setting clear targets and ensuring their implementation, and stresses the need to be true in word and resolute in deed, which will continue to provide valuable stability and certainty for global climate governance, Han said.

China has worked with the United Nations to advance international cooperation on addressing climate change, firmly upholding and fully implementing the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement, vigorously promoting South-South cooperation on climate change, and actively supporting the UN-led Early Warnings for All initiative, he said.

The global response to climate change currently faces numerous challenges, Han said, noting that developing countries, in particular, are confronted with difficulties including funding shortages, technological shortcomings and inadequate capacity in implementing their nationally determined contributions, which require the international community to address together.
China looks forward to seeing the 31st meeting make new progress and reach new consensus under the leadership of Guterres, he added.
Guterres asked Han to convey his sincere greetings to Xi.

Calling China an important pillar of multilateralism and a key supporter of the United Nations, Guterres said that China has walked the talk in addressing climate change, with its actions consistently going beyond its commitments.
As a global leader in renewable energy, China has made substantial contributions to reducing global greenhouse gas emissions, he said.
The global response to climate change is currently at a difficult juncture, and the United Nations looks to China for strong contributions and support in advancing global climate action, he said.

Guterres expressed the hope that the United Nations and China would further strengthen coordination, working together to ensure that the 31st meeting sends a positive signal to the world and makes joint decisions and concerted efforts needed to effectively reverse the trend of rising global temperatures and better address the challenges of climate change.

items.title: Large yellow croaker industry thrives in Ningde, SE China's Fujian
text: Journalists on a joint reporting tour for the 2026 Media Cooperation Forum on Belt and Road visit a large yellow croaker farming base in Ningde city, southeast China's Fujian Province. (People's Daily Online/Jiao Yan)
Large yellow croakers are thriving in deeper waters off Ningde city, southeast China's Fujian Province, thanks in part to three decades of support from the Agricultural Bank of China.

Guanjingyang, located in Sandu'ao, is the country's only natural inner-bay spawning ground for large yellow croakers. Rows of wind- and wave-resistant deep-water cages stretch across the bay. Ningde produces four out of every five farmed large yellow croakers in China, and the output value of its large yellow croaker industry chain has exceeded 20 billion yuan (about $3 billion).

"In the past, we relied on experience, judging conditions by water color and the weather, and often couldn't react in time to oxygen shortages or disease. Now data speaks, and risks are much easier to control," said Song Xiangguo, who manages a farming platform at Baiji Bay for a leading large yellow croaker breeding company.

The company's 84 standardized cages each measure 24 meters by 24 meters and are 12 meters deep, with a footprint of nearly one mu (about 0.07 hectares). Sensors monitor water temperature, dissolved oxygen, salinity and pH around the clock, uploading real-time data to the cloud, where it can be viewed on mobile phones, with alerts triggered when readings fall outside normal ranges. A deep-water cage yields 40 to 50 tonnes of fish a year, compared with 20 to 30 tonnes from a traditional small cage.
A foreign journalist tries feeding large yellow croakers on a farming platform in Ningde city, southeast China's Fujian Province. (People's Daily Online/Jiao Yan)
Financial support has helped drive the digital, eco-friendly and standardized development of the city's large yellow croaker industry.

In 1994, soon after a breakthrough in artificial breeding technology for the species, the company's predecessor secured a 300,000-yuan loan from the Agricultural Bank of China, marking its first step toward large-scale farming.

After a strong typhoon destroyed the company's farming platforms in 1996, the bank extended a 500,000-yuan working capital loan, assessing the company based on its technology and growth prospects rather than relying solely on collateral. In 2018, as Ningde began a campaign to clean up marine aquaculture, the bank's local branch provided nearly 70 million yuan to help replace old farming platforms, build new cages and install a smart system.

"Offshore farming has no collateral, runs on long cycles and is vulnerable to natural disasters. The bank looks at the technology, the team and the prospects of the industry chain. We began supporting the company at its start-up stage and have grown with it step by step," said Shi Zhiping, president of the bank's Ningde branch, explaining why the bank was willing to lend.

items.title: Chinese FM holds talks with Slovak counterpart
text: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, holds talks with Slovakia's Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Juraj Blanar in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 10, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Ling)
BEIJING, Nov. 10 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi held talks with Slovakia's Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Juraj Blanar in Beijing on Tuesday.

Noting that in recent years, under the guidance of the two countries' leaders, the China-Slovakia strategic partnership has maintained high-level momentum, Wang said the relationship has become a model for countries of different sizes and systems to coexist in friendship, treat each other as equals and pursue win-win cooperation.

Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, briefed the Slovak side on the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee. He said that China is ready to enhance experience sharing with Slovakia on party and state governance, make good use of mechanisms such as the intergovernmental cooperation committee, and increase people-to-people and grassroots exchanges.

China is ready to work with Slovakia to act on the vision of global governance featuring extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits and jointly build a community with a shared future for humanity, Wang said.

China always believes that China and Europe should remain committed to properly resolving frictions and differences through dialogue and consultation, and hopes Slovakia will continue to play a constructive role in the sound and steady development of China-Europe relations, Wang noted.

Blanar congratulated China on the successful convening of the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee, saying that the overall leadership of the Party and long-term political and social stability are the institutional strength and political guarantee behind China's sustained and rapid development. Slovakia is ready to strengthen inter-party exchanges with China, he added.

Blanar noted that Slovakia firmly adheres to the one-China policy and always regards China as an important partner. Slovakia will continue to do its utmost to provide a stable and sound environment for Chinese enterprises to invest and cooperate in the country and offer greater facilitation for personnel exchanges, he said.

Slovakia is also ready to play a constructive role in Europe-China dialogue and cooperation and will continue to support and take part in China-Central and Eastern European Countries cooperation, Blanar added.

items.title: China, France should strengthen dialogue, jointly address challenges, says FM
text: BEIJING, Nov. 10 (Xinhua) -- China and France should strengthen dialogue and cooperation, consolidate political mutual trust, and jointly address various risks and challenges, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said on Tuesday.

During a phone conversation with French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Jean-Noel Barrot, Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, noted that China and France are both founding members of the United Nations and permanent members of the UN Security Council.

The two countries' maintaining communication and strengthening coordination on developments and changes in the international situation are important for safeguarding the international system with the United Nations at its core, Wang said.

China is ready to work with France to fulfill their special responsibilities as permanent members of the UN Security Council and safeguard the common interests of the international community, he said.

Maintaining the healthy and stable development of China-France relations serves the interests of both countries and the international community, Wang said, calling on both sides to implement the consensus reached by the two heads of state.
He expressed the hope that France would honor its commitment to the one-China principle through concrete actions and safeguard the political foundation of China-France relations.

China and the European Union (EU) stand to gain from cooperation and lose from confrontation, Wang said, calling on the EU to work with China to build stable and balanced trade ties as key trading partners.
Wang said he believes that France, as a core EU member state, would play a constructive role in this regard.
For his part, Barrot said France has consistently attached great importance to China's status as a major country and remains committed to the one-China policy.

France hopes to maintain high-level engagement with China, deepen strategic mutual trust, and strengthen communication and coordination on such major issues as UN affairs and artificial intelligence, in order to jointly uphold multilateralism, safeguard global security and stability, and promote common development and prosperity, he said.
France stands ready to play an active role in fostering dialogue and cooperation between the EU and China, Barrot said.
The two sides also exchanged views on other issues of common concern, including the election of UN secretary-general.

items.title: China's solar industry helps curb global emissions
text: China's photovoltaic industry helped the world avoid about 4.91 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions between 2015 and 2025, while reducing global solar module procurement costs by an estimated $175.3 billion from 2011 to 2025, according to a report released in Beijing on Wednesday.

The report comes as COP31 continues in Antalya, Turkiye, where the Turkish presidency is promoting the conference as an "Implementation COP", focused on turning climate pledges and targets into measurable action on the ground.
Officially known as the 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, COP31 opened on Monday and will run through Nov 20.

Jointly published by the Chinese Research Academy of Environmental Sciences and the Institute of Public and Environmental Affairs, the report assesses the industry's contribution to global climate action through two independent measures: avoided emissions and cost savings.

It found that solar modules exported by China and installed domestically between 2015 and 2025 could help avoid a combined 37.78 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions over an assumed 25-year operating life.

During the period, China exported modules with a combined capacity of about 1,217.4 gigawatts, which had already helped avoid an estimated 2.14 billion metric tons of emissions overseas. Meanwhile, domestic installations totaling 1,175.3 GW had avoided another 2.77 billion metric tons.

The report also examined the "learning effect" — cost reductions resulting from accumulated production and deployment experience. Such experience enables manufacturers to address production problems, improve product yields and material efficiency, and optimize manufacturing processes and supply chain management.
It estimated that the learning effect associated with China's accumulated module exports had made global solar module prices in 2025 about 23.2 percent lower than they otherwise would have been.

As a result, global buyers saved an estimated $175.3 billion on module purchases between 2011 and 2025, including $83.39 billion in overseas markets. Nearly 73 percent of the savings occurred between 2022 and 2025, as global solar deployment expanded rapidly.
The report noted that the estimate covers module procurement costs rather than total project investment, which also includes financing, land, grid connections, installation and maintenance.
It said affordable solar power could help support the COP31 presidency's "35 by 35" initiative, which seeks to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035.

The report called for stronger international cooperation on installation tracking, power generation data and assessment methods to enable more transparent and widely recognized evaluations of the climate contributions of clean technologies.

items.title: Chilled lamb gets a fast ride to Macao
text: The first shipment of fresh chilled lamb produced in Guangdong province was loaded onto trucks under the supervision of customs officers in Zhuhai and moved to Macao on Tuesday.
It was the first time refrigerated local lamb from the province had been supplied to Macao, offering more choices for residents there.
Previously, refrigerated lamb in the Macao market mainly came from processing enterprises in the Inner Mongolia autonomous region, Hebei province and other parts of the Chinese mainland.
Zhuhai Runhe Food Co became the first company in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area to qualify to supply it to Macao, building on its earlier experience with pork.
After live sheep enter the facility, they undergo six processes — cleaning, slaughtering, cutting, acid removal, cooling and packaging, Wang Wenwu, general manager of Zhuhai Runhehe Food Co said.
"Once they pass customs inspection and quarantine, they can be shipped to Macao in less than 12 hours, ensuring maximum freshness," Wang said.
At full capacity, the company will supply more than 1.8 tons of chilled lamb to Macao weekly.
Customs in Zhuhai has offered full-day appointment-based inspections, rapid certification and immediate release upon inspection to ensure that the lamb is efficiently tested and shipped.

As of Monday, Doumen Customs, a part of Gongbei Customs, has inspected and released 58 shipments of chilled pork totaling 27.85 metric tons and three of chilled beef totaling 250 kilograms for supply to Macao.

items.title: China leads clean energy adoption as global emissions hit record levels
text: China's carbon dioxide emissions are projected to decrease by 0.9 percent in 2026, following two years of low emissions growth, according to the 2026 Global Carbon Budget. In addition to a strong decrease in oil emissions, coal emissions are projected to rise slightly by 0.3 percent, while electricity generation from renewables continues to grow strongly.

China produces 32 percent of global fossil emissions, but it is also the country most active in deploying clean technologies and increasing carbon sinks through reforestation. Half of the global emissions avoided due to renewable energy and electric vehicles are in China. The country also has the largest carbon uptake through reforestation and afforestation.

Globally, fossil CO2 emissions are projected to reach 38.2 billion metric tons and total emissions to rise to 43.3 billion tons this year. While energy demand continues to rise, two-thirds of the increase is being met by increased solar and wind power and electric vehicles. However, clean energy growth is yet to account for a durable decline in global fossil CO2 emissions.

The analysis published alongside the report in Nature Climate Change found that emissions avoided by solar and wind power rose from 0.28 billion tons in 2010 to 4.1 billion tons in 2025, and are projected to reach 4.6 billion tons in 2026.
Clean technologies are making a real difference in reducing global emissions, said Professor Corinne Le Quere, Royal Society Research Professor at the University of East Anglia.

"Solar and wind power and electric vehicles are expanding rapidly, led by China. Countries on every continent are decreasing their emissions while growing their economies. A further acceleration could turn the tide on global emissions within a few years," she said.

items.title: Japan's views on history raise concern
text: Critics in Japan have raised concerns that some entertainment productions distort history, while historical sites fail to adequately address Japan's wartime aggression and responsibility for its atrocities.
Such portrayals and omissions, they warn, risk undermining public understanding of the past. They have called for stronger history education and a more honest reckoning with Japan's wartime actions.

The second season of Japanese TV drama Vivant, which has come under fire for its negative portrayal of China and alleged promotion of anti-Chinese sentiment, ended on Sunday. Broadcaster TBS has announced that a film adaptation will be released nationwide next month.

Criticism of the series has centered on its depiction of Chinese intelligence agents as brutal torturers and its attribution of methods once used by Japanese troops during the invasion of China to present-day Chinese characters, effectively reversing the historical roles of perpetrators and victims.

Masahiko Yamashita, professor emeritus at Tokai University in Tokyo, described such portrayals as absurd and deeply troubling. He questioned how a drama could claim to be fictional while naming real countries and presenting its story as though it reflected reality.

The season finale carried disclaimers at both the beginning and the end, stating that the story was entirely fictional, was not intended to incite violence or hostility between nations, and was intended to convey respect for people of all countries and a desire for world peace.

Japanese media outlets, including Sports Nippon and Oricon News, described the disclaimers as unusual. Their reports also mentioned the controversy over the show's portrayal of China and Japanese entertainment giant Sanrio's earlier decision to end its collaboration with the series.

Japanese historian Masahiro Yamazaki criticized the coverage, saying on social media that it framed the controversy as "Chinese media questioning the portrayals" while ignoring widespread criticism within Japan.

He also warned of the potential impact of the upcoming film, likening the decision to proceed with a production containing anti-China content despite the backlash to the way Japan's former militarists launched wars of aggression.

Meanwhile, commercial tie-ins, merchandise sales and tourism promotions linked to Vivant continue. According to TBS, the series has launched at least 40 collaborations and promotional campaigns across aviation, railways, tourism, restaurants, clothing and retail, extending its reach into everyday life in Japan.
Beyond the concerns over Vivant, historians have highlighted the broader influence of popular culture on public perceptions of war.

Yutaka Yoshida, a historian and professor emeritus at Hitotsubashi University in Tokyo, said anime and other cultural works have helped foster pacifist attitudes in postwar Japan, perhaps even more than textbooks.
However, understanding war through popular culture requires solid historical knowledge and deep reflection, he said. Without these, such works risk distorting public perceptions of history.

items.title: How the CPC plans to sustain its anti-corruption drive
text: BEIJING -- China has pledged to sustain its anti-graft drive in key sectors and target new and concealed forms of corruption, including those through virtual currency and cross-border financial activities.

At a key Party plenum held in late October, the Communist Party of China Central Committee adopted a resolution on persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance, underscoring the Party's resolve to maintain a tough stance against corruption and strengthen oversight over the exercise of power.

Since the 20th CPC National Congress held in 2022, the Party has stepped up its fight against corruption in key sectors including finance, State-owned enterprises, energy, tobacco, pharmaceuticals, and project bidding and tendering.
Special campaigns have also been reinforced to address corruption in grain procurement and sales, as well as in the football sector.

The resolution pledged to investigate and deal with cases involving both political and economic issues, collusion between government officials and businesspeople, and capital penetrating into the political domain.

It also vowed to crack down hard on graft of the "key few," especially officials in top posts, and young officials, and take stern action against corruption committed by leading officials' families and staff.

Over the years, some senior officials — including former members of the Political Bureau and its Standing Committee, senior military officials, former government ministers, and retirees who left their leading positions years ago — have been brought to justice for violations of law.

In February 2026, revised regulations were issued to strengthen oversight of leaders of SOEs, prohibiting them from abusing power, engaging in unauthorized commercial activities or investments, and practicing nepotism or favoritism.

At a news conference on the guiding principles from the October plenum, a senior anti-graft official said the CPC had outlined priorities for steadfastly following a distinctive Chinese path to combating corruption.

They include maintaining a tough anti-graft stance, strengthening oversight of power, fostering a culture of integrity, and enhancing coordinated efforts to prevent corruption by rooting out audacity, opportunity, and desire, said Zhang Fuhai, deputy secretary of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection of the CPC and deputy head of the National Commission of Supervision.

The resolution pledged to target new and disguised forms of corruption such as receiving returns later for abusing one's power for the beneficiaries, reaping benefits from assets under the name of bribe givers or a third party, the "white glove" or agents concealing corruption activities in ostensibly legal forms, and the "revolving door" phenomenon of bureaucrat-merchant collusion after officials' retirement.
Such offenses feature increasingly concealed actors, diversified channels for illicit benefit transfers, and more obscured connections between power and money.

items.title: New rockets to lift nation's launch capacity
text: A major Chinese space enterprise is developing two new carrier rocket models and plans to conduct their debut flights next year, according to a top company official.

Speaking on Monday at a commercial space forum in Wuhan, Hubei province, Zha Xiongquan, chairman of Expace Technology, said the company is developing the Kuaizhou 6 and Kuaizhou 12 rockets to meet the country's rapidly growing demand for high-capacity launch vehicles.

"Expace has been leveraging mature technologies and existing production capacity to develop the Kuaizhou 12 — a low-cost medium-lift rocket that uses both solid and liquid propellants. It will have a launch cost of less than 20,000 yuan ($3,000) per kilogram," Zha said.

The Kuaizhou 12 is scheduled to make its debut flight and enter commercial service in 2027. Its introduction is expected to help China's space industry break the bottleneck in low-cost, large-scale launch capacity.
Zha said the company is also accelerating development of the reusable Kuaizhou 6 liquid-fueled rocket, which is on track to complete its first orbital flight and first-stage recovery next year.

According to Expace designers, the Kuaizhou 12 will be about 47 meters tall and have a fairing diameter of 5.2 meters. It will be capable of carrying 10 metric tons of payload to a typical low-Earth orbit.

The Kuaizhou 6 will be much taller at 73 meters, and it will have a booster diameter of 4.5 meters. In a nonrecoverable mission, the rocket will be able to carry 18 tons of payload to a low-Earth orbit. For reusable flights, which involve recovery of the first-stage booster, it will be able to carry 14 tons to the same orbit.

The Kuaizhou is China's leading solid-propellant rocket series, in contrast to the Long March family, which relies mainly on liquid propellants. To date, the two main Kuaizhou models — 1A and 11 — have completed 37 flights, deploying nearly 100 satellites into space.
Zha said at the forum that the Kuaizhou 1A and Kuaizhou 11 are expected to carry out more than 50 launches over the next three years.

"Through regular, high-frequency launch services, these rockets will further cement the country's global lead in space rapid-response capabilities and support national emergency-response requirements," he said.

items.title: ‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019249/‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
text: “Sisters, stand up!” reads a slogan written in pink on the mirror above three pink-and-white urinals. Alongside each sits a stack of disposable paper funnels, waiting for those willing to heed the call.

The scene, reportedly captured in the women’s restroom of a bar in China’s eastern city of Wuxi, began circulating online last week, sparking debate and prompting a related hashtag to garner over 54 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Tuesday.

“I stood there in disbelief for two minutes, thinking I’d walked into the wrong restroom,” one user wrote on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, attaching photos of the urinals. “I kept checking until a cleaner confirmed it was indeed the women’s restroom.”

The user, a Wuxi resident in her 30s surnamed Shi, told domestic media she was unsure how to use the urinals as there were no instructions nearby. She said she eventually opted for a traditional squat toilet in the same restroom instead because she worried about making a mess or soiling her clothes.
“I’d actually love to try this,” one commenter wrote. “In winter, it’s a hassle to squat with all those thick, long layers on, especially when you’re also carrying a bag.”
“Better yet, let the brothers sit down,” read another comment, which received nearly 1,400 likes.

On Tuesday, a woman surnamed Tang, who runs Gungun Folk Theater, the bar where the urinals were reportedly installed, told domestic media that they were intended for women who find it difficult to squat, including those wearing long dresses or with limited mobility. “We just wanted to make things easier and give women another option,” she said.

Studies suggest that standing to urinate may be easier for pregnant women and those with knee osteoarthritis, while standing, crouching, and sitting have been found to make no significant difference to bladder emptying in healthy women.
Standing urinals are increasingly common worldwide at music festivals to save space and reduce restroom queues, and at outdoor activities where toilets are scarce.

In China, efforts to introduce standing urinals for women reportedly date back to 2004. At that time, Ye Ganlin, a retired senior engineer, spent 10,000 yuan ($1,400) developing a portable standing urinal for all genders, and offered free disposable funnels to female users. She said the idea grew out of her own experience with a spinal condition that made squatting increasingly difficult as she aged.

Her toilet was tested in busy public areas of neighboring cities Xi’an and Xianyang, in the northwestern Shaanxi province, and reportedly drew around 200 users a day. However, women were in the minority, Ye said.

In 2010, Shaanxi Normal University, also in Xi’an, installed six standing urinals for women, an initiative championed by professor Qu Yajun to conserve water. Female students welcomed the idea but said it would take practice to get used to the fixtures.
(Header image: Urinals installed in a women’s restroom at a bar in Wuxi, Jiangsu province, October 2026. From Weibo)

items.title: Collage: Robots, Health and New Tech at China Expo
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019251/Collage: Robots, Health and New Tech at China Expo
text: SHANGHAI — The ninth China International Import Expo ran from Nov. 5 to 10, with 4,142 overseas exhibitors from 162 countries, regions and international organizations.

More than 480 exhibits made global, Asian or Chinese debuts. Qualcomm brought a 6G terminal prototype out of the lab. Medtronic’s China-developed Kanghui orthopedic surgical robot had its world premiere. And a rare type of durian tree fruit, the Malaysian white durian, made its global debut.

Robots at the expo could be found working hotel front desks, taking photos for visitors, and running booth demos on their own — visibly more advanced than in past years. In place of the mechanical arm designed to play ping-pong featured last year, at this year’s expo, a company debuted an entire humanoid robot playing the sport. At the forum held alongside the expo, Xiong Jijun, Vice Minister of Industry and Information Technology, said humanoid robots must be upgraded from performing simple actions to being “able to think and work.”
Sixth Tone photographers spent the week in the halls, capturing the new products, technologies and services on display.

items.title: From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019240/From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
text: The ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) closed in Shanghai on Tuesday after showcasing cutting-edge technologies in artificial intelligence, commercial aerospace, and innovative drugs.

The six-day event drew exhibitors from a record 162 countries, regions, and international organizations. A total of 4,142 overseas companies took part — also a record high — with more than 480 representative products making their global, Asian, or China debut.

U.S. wireless chipmaker Qualcomm exhibited the world’s first 6G terminal prototype — the first time the device has been shown publicly outside the lab. The prototype has been used in joint tests with China Mobile, China’s largest telecom operator, and Chinese telecom equipment manufacturer ZTE. The prototype will provide the foundation for 6G chips and support the technology’s commercial rollout.

The event featured an expanded medical devices and health care exhibition area, acting as the stage for the China debut of pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca’s new hypertension medication baxdrostat. The oral medication works by inhibiting the enzyme aldosterone synthase, which helps synthesize the blood pressure-regulating hormone aldosterone, and was approved in the U.S. in May.

German optical giant Zeiss also made its global debut of its new non-spherical lens PT Lunana, designed for myopia correction. Novartis, a Swiss multinational pharmaceutical company, showcased ianalumab, a drug used for treating the autoimmune illness Sjögren’s disease — also a China debut.

American electric vehicle company Tesla presented its Cybercab autonomous vehicle. Lacking a steering wheel or pedals, the vehicle relies on cameras and AI to drive. Hexagon — a global digital reality and metrology tech company — also displayed its industrial humanoid robot AEON.

Aerospace technology was also present, including the Zhuque-3 rocket developed by Chinese commercial aerospace company LandSpace. The rocket’s reusable booster, which uses liquid oxygen and methane as fuel, can land vertically, first achieved by the company in August.

Beyond showcasing new tech, the expo held its first exhibition area for 100 long-established, reputable international brands — from Canadian shoe companies to Spanish wineries — as well as hosted a trade and investment “matchmaking” conference, where companies and buyers met to sign cooperation agreements. The latter conference attracted more than 600 exhibitors and over 2,000 buyers from 59 countries and regions.
The deals reached at this year’s expo are projected to be worth a total of $85.45 billion over the coming year, up 2.3% from last year and a record high.

items.title: Postscript: China Opens School Dedicated to Ancient Chinese Writing
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019239/Postscript: China Opens School Dedicated to Ancient Chinese Writing
text: China has opened its first school dedicated to declining and obscure fields of study, with a focus on ancient and classical Chinese texts.

The School for Rare and Endangered Disciplines was inaugurated in Beijing on Nov. 6 under the University of Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (UCASS). At the opening, the university also announced the launch of a national alliance of more than 80 universities, museums, and cultural and research institutions to share resources, conduct collaborative research, and cultivate talent in related fields.

The school comes as the number of scholars studying ancient Chinese scripts dwindles. Nationwide, only about 500 people work in ancient Chinese writing studies, and of the roughly 4,500 known oracle bone characters — the oldest known fully developed form of Chinese writing and widely used for divination purposes during the Shang dynasty (c.1600–1046 BC) — nearly two-thirds remain undeciphered, underlining the need for further research.

The initiative also builds on previous attempts by UCASS to preserve such fields, such as establishing an institute for rare and endangered studies in 2024 to train future talent in fields such as bamboo and silk studies, which examines script on the two materials, as well as classical studies, Turkic studies, and Assyriology, or studies of the Ancient Near East.

Each student of the new school’s bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degree courses will be mentored by two members of the school’s more than 140 faculty members. UCASS has also built dedicated laboratories for the school’s use.

Students may pursue research in oracle bone studies, bamboo and silk studies, and classical studies. They may also train in over 10 ancient ethnic scripts, including Turkic, Tangut, Khitan, Jurchen, Manchu, Old Tibetan, Old Yi, Phags-pa, Naxi Dongba, and Zhuang.

“Ancient scripts like oracle bone script are on the verge of being lost, and some frontier history research relies on the survival of the country’s cultural roots and its long-term development,” Huang Dekuan, director of the Research and Conservation Center for Unearthed Texts at Tsinghua University, told state broadcaster CCTV.
Such disciplines are also hampered by scattered resources and research institutions working in isolation — key obstacles to research and transmission, according to CCTV.

China has called for increased focus on cultural heritage preservation in recent years. At an October press conference on cultural heritage protection, government officials called for advancing cultural heritage as a discipline, cultivating interdisciplinary talent in the field, and encouraging qualified universities to establish cultural heritage schools.

In a Nov. 7 commentary, domestic media outlet The Beijing News wrote that by emphasizing rare and endangered disciplines, the new school offers a lesson to other universities: schools should develop their own distinctive majors, resist the urge to offer only popular fields, and actively strengthen less mainstream majors.
“Only then can a university truly serve education,” it stated.

items.title: Fallback to First Choice: Why Chinese Parents Are Rethinking Vocational Schools
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019245/Fallback to First Choice: Why Chinese Parents Are Rethinking Vocational Schools
text: Coming from a Shanghai family with a strong academic background, Yang Fan had always felt studying at university was his destiny. The only problem was, he was flunking middle school.

“He’d make the same mistake with a character the entire semester. I just couldn’t get him to do it right,” says his mother, Zhao Xuan, who could only look on in frustration as Yang struggled with his homework night after night. “Given how much it was taking for him to get through middle school, I felt high school would crush him.”

Last summer, with the conventional academic pathway looking a bad fit for their 15-year-old son, Zhao and her husband began to consider China’s integrated secondary vocational-to-undergraduate articulation program. Launched as a 2014 pilot in Shanghai, the initiative sees students spend up to three years at a vocational school before transitioning to a partner university to complete a related four-year bachelor’s degree program.
Over the past 12 years, the number of participating educational institutions has rapidly expanded, now covering at least seven provincial regions, and applications have soared.

Shanghai alone has established 91 majors across 38 vocational schools and 18 universities, enrolling about 20,000 students and producing six cohorts of graduates. Planned enrollment this year was 2,756, up from just 120 in 2014 and a 17.5% increase from 2025.

Programs cover diverse fields including robotics, accounting, digital media arts, big data engineering, logistics, environmental design, hospitality management, cultural heritage restoration, smart manufacturing, performing arts, sound recording, information security, and materials science.

The trend reflects a sea change in attitudes toward vocational education in China. Technical skills training has long been stigmatized as “low status” and a “fallback option,” but as the country’s workforce undergoes a massive restructuring driven by an aging population, advancements in artificial intelligence, and an economic slowdown, more people feel it now makes students more employable compared to those with purely academic backgrounds.

In real terms, most students in the integrated program say their experiences are far less stressful than those of their peers at traditional Chinese high schools, and that they are encouraged to focus more on their personal strengths rather than sticking to a one-size-fits-all curriculum.

However, because most applicants are only in their mid-teens, it’s often parents who make the final decision, with research suggesting that more-passive children have only a vague idea of, or interest in, what might lie ahead.

It was only when Zhao learned that the prestigious Shanghai Maritime University (SMU) would join the integrated secondary vocational-to-undergraduate articulation program in 2026 that she was sure the pathway was a “realistic match” for Yang.

items.title: More Chinese Regions to Require Autumn and Spring School Breaks
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019236/More Chinese Regions to Require Autumn and Spring School Breaks
text: More Chinese regions are implementing autumn and spring breaks in compulsory education, expanding a decadelong national initiative. Some have also waived fees for students on break and rolled out support measures to help parents take leave at the same time as their children.

Spring and autumn holidays across all compulsory education schools have been rolled out provincewide in at least 15 provinces, as well as numerous cities in other provinces, such as the southern megacity of Shenzhen, domestic media reported last week. In China, compulsory education lasts nine years, encompassing primary and middle school. Breaks will occur in November and April for four to five days each.

The reform dates back to 2004, when Hangzhou, capital of the eastern province of Zhejiang, piloted the breaks. In 2013, the initiative expanded nationally when the State Council issued an announcement encouraging local governments to adopt it, and the rollout accelerated again in 2025 when central authorities urged more schools to implement the holidays.
Chu Zhaohui, a researcher at the China National Academy of Educational Sciences, told domestic media outlet Red Star News that the holidays actually boost learning.
“Learning isn’t confined to schools or taught only by teachers and parents,” Chu said, adding that the holidays give students space for self-exploration.

At the same time as introducing spring and autumn holiday policies, many cities have also added supporting measures so parents can sync their leave. In October, Longnan city in the northwestern Gansu province encouraged employers to implement paid leave and prioritize compensatory rest for employees with school-age children, aligning staff leave with school holidays.

Foshan, a city in the southern Guangdong province, also issued a proposal on Nov. 3 calling on employers to prioritize arranging leave for employees with children during the autumn holiday. The city’s five-day autumn break begins Nov. 11.

Many tourist spots are also waiving entrance fees for children during the upcoming fall break. In the eastern city of Wuxi, a theme park dropped entry fees for students 16 and under throughout November; 15 top tourism sites in Huangshan in the eastern Anhui province, a city known for its mountain of the same name, are now entry-free for children under 18; and the Dujiangyan scenic area in the southwestern Sichuan province waived fees for primary and middle school students between Nov. 12 and 16.

The breaks have significantly boosted travel demand, according to online travel booking platform Qunar. Data from Qunar revealed that in November, air ticket bookings for children 12 and under increased 1.6 times year on year, while parent bookings rose by 50%.

Wang Qiyan, director of the Leisure Economy Research Center at Renmin University, told Red Star News that spring and autumn breaks “enable off-peak travel, avoiding the packed scenic spots of winter and summer vacations.
(Header image: Tourists take photos of St. Sophia Square during the autumn break in Harbin, Heilongjiang province, Nov. 4, 2026. VCG)

items.title: A Bad Review, a Suicide, and a Debate Over Cyberbullying in China
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019228/A Bad Review, a Suicide, and a Debate Over Cyberbullying in China
text: On Oct. 6, 2026, a female customer posted complaints on multiple social media platforms about a fried skewer stall in Gao County, Yibin, in southwestern China’s Sichuan province. “Avoid XX Copper Pot Potatoes. The owner can’t take the heat,” she wrote. She had bought a 10-yuan ($1.40) fried food combo from the stall, run by a 33-year-old woman surnamed Hu, but was dissatisfied with the portion of potatoes. “She just refused to add potatoes afterward,” the customer added. Her location-tagged posts quickly spread, and negative comments about Hu and her stall flooded the comment sections.
Hu responded to the criticism, writing, “I stand behind my portions.” Three days later, on Oct. 9, she jumped into a river and died by suicide.

Hu had run the stall for more than four years, sleeping less than six hours a night. In her suicide note, she described the enormous pressures she faced in life. She had hoped to watch her child grow up, she wrote, but the video telling people to avoid her stall had been the straw that broke the camel’s back.

She also wrote: “These past two days I have experienced what I consider cyberbullying. One person complained about no potatoes in her order, and then the comments came flooding in about bad service and poor-tasting food.”

This was not the first tragedy of its kind. In August 2025, a 57-year-old obstetrician-gynecologist surnamed Shao in Zhoukou, central China’s Henan province, jumped to her death. According to her family, she had endured more than seven months of cyberbullying over a medical dispute. In 2023, after a primary school student in Wuhan, capital of the central Hubei province, was killed in a traffic accident on campus, his mother was subjected to online attacks and later jumped to her death. In cases like these, public opinion often attributes the tragedies to cyberbullying.
But in Hu’s case, labeling the entire incident “cyberbullying” and placing the blame on the customer who posted the negative review would exaggerate the power of a single act of expression.

The customer maintained that she was simply describing a genuine experience, with “no malice, incitement, or falsehood.” She did not insult or personally attack anyone, disclose private information, or call for coordinated attacks online or offline. Her criticism may have been harsh, subjective, or exaggerated, but based on the content of her posts alone, it is difficult to characterize it as cyberbullying.

Many negative comments about the stall owner appeared beneath the posts, but there is currently no evidence that they were all malicious. Public criticism can be harsh, but legal liability must rest on provable facts.

In July 2026, China released a draft Anti-Online Violence Law for public comment. It defines online violence as “concentrated or sustained” acts involving “insult and abuse, rumor-mongering and defamation, incitement of hatred,” and similar behavior. A negative review based on a genuine transaction cannot automatically be classified as cyberbullying because it has harmful consequences. Moreover, the draft has not yet become law.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: China's NEV exports surge 144.7% in Oct, growth expected to moderate as overseas markets mature
text: China's new-energy vehicle (NEV) exports surged 144.7 percent year-on-year in October, industry data showed on Monday, underscoring strong overseas demand even as domestic sales weakened. Industry analysts said that exports are likely to maintain robust momentum in the near term, although growth is likely to moderate as overseas markets mature and competition intensifies.

Chinese producers exported 582,000 passenger NEVs in October, up 3.9 percent from September, according to data released by the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA). Meanwhile, domestic NEV retail sales fell 13.7 percent year-on-year to 1.109 million units, although they rose 2.3 percent month-on-month.
Cui Dongshu, secretary-general of the CPCA, told the Global Times on Monday that China's automobile exports are expected to shift from rapid growth this year to a more moderate pace in 2027.

Cui forecast that overall vehicle export growth could slow to about 10 percent next year as shipments to Russia stabilize and exports to the EU face mounting pressure. The Middle East region could provide additional growth, although prospects remain uncertain, he said.
Passenger NEV exports reached 4.472 million units in the first 10 months of 2026, up 139.7 percent year-on-year, according to the CPCA.

These figures also point to a changing export structure. NEVs accounted for 62.8 percent of China's passenger vehicle exports in October, up 20 percentage points from a year earlier. Battery electric vehicles represented 61.7 percent of NEV shipments, while conventional plug-in hybrids accounted for 33.7 percent.

Leading Chinese automakers recorded substantial overseas shipments. BYD exported 165,194 passenger NEVs in October, followed by Chery with 83,843 and Geely with 80,119, CPCA figures showed. Tesla China's exports reached 59,012 units.

Zhang Xiang, a researcher at the Automotive Industry Innovation Research Center of North China University of Technology, told the Global Times on Monday that Chinese automakers have established a competitive edge in the global NEV market through technological advances, mature supply chains and increasingly competitive products.

He said that he expects overseas demand to remain strong in the coming months, supporting continued export growth. However, as NEV adoption expands and initial demand is gradually absorbed, export growth is likely to return to a more sustainable pace over the longer term.

The expansion comes amid a changing international trade environment. The EU has imposed additional countervailing duties on China-made battery electric vehicles, while Chinese manufacturers are increasingly exploring emerging markets to diversify their overseas sales.

According to the International Energy Agency, sales of Chinese-made electric cars last year grew by 130 percent in Southeast Asia, 60 percent in the Middle East and 55 percent in Latin America, highlighting growing demand beyond traditional markets.

items.title: Singapore Business Federation leads 54 firms to CIIE to unlock bilateral and regional opportunities
text: Singapore firms continue to value China as an important market, and the Southeast Asian country's extensive business networks and familiarity with Southeast Asian markets make it a valuable partner for Chinese enterprises looking to expand their regional footprint, an executive of the Singapore Business Federation said.

China remains a significant market for Singapore businesses, underpinned by its vast consumer market, evolving demand and focus on high-quality development, Mark Lee, chairman of SBF, said during an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the ongoing 9th China International Import Expo held in Shanghai on Friday.

The federation is leading a delegation of 54 Singapore firms to the CIIE. Since the inaugural CIIE in 2018, Singapore businesses have generated about 2.79 billion yuan ($420 million) in cumulative trade value through the event.

Spanning established household names and emerging businesses, participating Singaporean firms at the expo highlight the country's competitive strength in food, health and wellness, consumer innovation, financial services and professional solutions.

They include See Hai Tat Medical Hall (Singapore) Pte Ltd, which looks to grow its consumer presence in China, and Prima Food Pte Ltd, which wants to use the CIIE to explore opportunities in the Chinese market.

With Singapore set to be the ASEAN chair in 2027, the SBF's participation in the CIIE this year — as it has done across all previous editions of the expo — further highlights its role as a strategic bridge for Chinese enterprises looking to expand into the ASEAN market, Lee said.

"Singapore features transparent, trusted legal frameworks and strong intellectual property protection, which helps safeguard technology rights as solutions expand into ASEAN and other regions. We are also a financing hub," Lee said, adding that this explains why many of the country's professional services partners are at the CIIE. They include banks, advisory firms, human resources consultants, legal service providers and trade compliance specialists.

He highlighted that China is among the global leaders in AI and digitization. Singaporean businesses want to work closely and conduct business with their Chinese counterparts, and such collaborations are already underway.

Lee raised the example of Pony.ai, a Chinese autonomous vehicle AI company, which partnered with ComfortDelGro, a Singaporean transport operator that runs taxi and fleet services. They launched a robotaxi pilot in China's Guangzhou, Guangdong province, and following the pilot, a robotaxi service was rolled out earlier this year in a designated area in Singapore, using Pony.ai's technology.

"ComfortDelGro stated that the pilot supports its broader global strategy covering China and Singapore, since it provides fleet management services across multiple markets. This illustrates a strong model: proven Chinese technology, localized by Singapore companies, with plans to scale into other regions and countries," Lee said.
Singapore and China share longstanding economic ties, with bilateral trade in goods reaching approximately 895.9 billion yuan last year

items.title: Austrian chocolate maker Zotter sees sweet opportunities at CIIE
text: This undated file photo shows an aerial view of Zotter's chocolate theater in Bergl, Austria. items.title: Record number of product debuts at CIIE highlights China’s emerging role as innovation hub
text: "Show China your best." That is the invitation the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) extends to the world. The response? More than 480 products and technologies making their global, Asian or China debuts, from 6G device prototypes and AI computing systems to innovative medicines, luxury skincare and fragrances - a vibrant showcase of global innovation meeting the energy of China's vast consumer market that is more open to new products and ideas.

For global companies, the CIIE is more than a showcase for new products. It is a window into China - one that opens onto a vast consumer market, an evolving innovation landscape and expanding opportunities for international cooperation. What comes through that window is not just a flow of goods, but a deeper exchange of ideas, technologies and opportunities.

At Qualcomm's booth in the Technology and Equipment Exhibition Area, visitors are lining up to see what the US chipmaker describes as the world's first 6G device prototype compliant with the latest 3GPP specifications. Making its global debut at the expo, the prototype is among the booth's main attractions.

Another new arrival is the large-model-native agent phone STEPX Neo, which integrates applications and services including Alipay, Jianying (CapCut) and Trip.com. Its combination of hardware, software and AI models points to how AI agents could become more closely integrated into everyday mobile services.

Intel is taking a different approach to the AI boom, focusing on where computing power is generated and how it is supplied. Its CIIE debut is a computing solution that places computing clusters inside shipping containers, with flexible energy storage modules, allowing them to operate closer to renewable energy sources.

"Rather than bringing electricity to computing centers, it makes more sense to move computing clusters closer to where the electricity is generated," Intel China Chairman Wang Zhicong told the Global Times.
The solution, first conceived as an idea at last year's expo, combines computing power, renewable energy and storage, with Chinese energy and IT companies involved in its development.

The exhibits are not confined to technology and equipment. In healthcare, Roche is presenting nearly 100 debut and first-show exhibits, including innovative medicines for breast cancer, lupus nephritis and other diseases. Boehringer Ingelheim is showcasing 14 innovative pipeline products and solutions in human pharmaceuticals and animal health, with three therapies at the forefront of global R&D making their China debut.

Both companies are also looking to deepen their engagement with China's medical innovation ecosystem. Vivian Bian, CEO of Roche Pharma China, told the Global Times that Roche will take the CIIE as an important fulcrum for open cooperation, continue to increase its local investment, and deeply integrate into China's medical innovation ecosystem.

items.title: Annual CIIE opens in Shanghai, showcasing China's commitment to opening up
text: On Thursday morning, in the waiting lounge of the opening ceremony of the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai, two hours before the ceremony began, the guests had already begun arriving.

They took selfies, chatted, posed for group photos with old friends and gave interviews to the media. According to on-site observations by the Global Times, in the relaxing atmosphere, the words they mentioned most were "opportunity", "openness" and "market."

Running from Thursday to Tuesday next week, this year's CIIE has attracted 4,142 overseas exhibitors, with total exhibition area exceeding 440,000 square meters. Over 480 exhibits are set to make their global, Asian or China debut at the event, the highest number in history. In addition, nearly 200 companies and institutions have been "full attendees" at the CIIE for all nine editions.

In his keynote speech at the opening ceremony, Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang, also a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, said that the CIIE has witnessed China's firm determination and concrete actions to promote high-standard opening-up, the remarkable results and tremendous gains of businesses and people from various countries in sharing opportunities in the Chinese market, and the unremitting efforts and important contributions of visionary people from all walks of life in improving global economic governance, according to Xinhua News Agency.

This fully demonstrates China's strategic resolve in advancing high-standard opening-up, injecting valuable certainty, stability and confidence in development into the world, Hu Qimu, professor at the Maritime Silk Road Institute of Huaqiao University, told the Global Times on Thursday.

Gabonese President Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, Federal Chancellor Christian Stocker of Austria, and UN Development Programme Administrator Alexander De Croo attended the opening ceremony and delivered remarks, Xinhua reported.

Ding's speech was welcomed by many executives from global multinational companies, who said they draw great inspiration from the speech and remain confident in honoring their long-term commitment to China.

Rogier Janssens, President of Merck China, told the Global Times that CIIE brings the world to China, and gives China a stronger voice in the global conversation. "As China moves into its 15th Five-Year Plan, the Expo's role is even more important," Janssens said.

The CIIE opening ceremony underscored the importance of openness, collaboration and innovation-driven development, further reinforcing Henkel's confidence in the long-term growth of the Chinese market, Anna An, President of Henkel China told the Global Times on Thursday.

Vice Premier Ding's speech reaffirmed China's steadfast commitment to high-standard opening-up and highlighted the country's important role in driving growth and building an open global economy, echoed Poh-Yian Koh, President of FedEx China.

items.title: Nissan CEO breaks down how it plans to fight back against Chinese companies, after second outlook cut in months
text: Nissan Motor plans to expand exports of vehicles developed in China to help compete against Chinese rivals globally, CEO Ivan Espinosa told CNBC on Wednesday.
The export push comes as intensifying competition in the world's largest auto market forced the company to cut its annual sales forecast for a second time in months.
Espinosa said Nissan would rapidly increase its exports of China-developed vehicles from two models to five, targeting 12 regional market clusters in the "very near term."

The Japanese automaker is responding to intensifying competition in China by developing vehicles specifically for Chinese consumers, using local technology, lower costs and faster development processes, he said.
"We can defend ourselves from these very aggressive players by using exactly the same elements that they have: speed, cost, and good technology," he told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe."
Nissan faces weakening demand and an accelerating shift toward electric vehicles in China, even as its restructuring efforts show progress in the U.S. and Japan.

On Wednesday, Nissan cut its global sales outlook for the fiscal year ending March 2027 to between 2.97 million and 3 million vehicles, down from 3.15 million previously. It maintained its full-year operating profit and net cash guidance.

In China, "weaker demand, a faster-than-anticipated shift to [new energy vehicles] and intensifying competition are putting greater pressure on sales than initially anticipated," the company said in a statement.
In August, Nissan revised its full-year sales volume outlook from 3.3 million units to 3.15 million units.
In October, shares of peer Volvo Cars crashed after it reported a swing to operating loss, citing tough market conditions in China and the U.S.
CEO Håkan Samuelsson told CNBC at the time that it needed a new strategy in China, with regionally adapted cars.

"It's really a lot about the Chinese market, of course, where the change has come faster than we thought, and really now we can see that selling global cars developed in Europe and China will not work, and then this is affecting all the Western players in China," Samuelsson said.
On Wednesday, Nissan also reported a 96% drop in second-quarter operating profit to 2.1 billion yen ($13 million), significantly below analyst expectations of 54.9 billion yen, according to FactSet.
The drop in profits was due to no longer having the benefit of lower U.S. emissions-related expenses that boosted profits a year ago, the company said.
Net revenue grew 8.2% to 3.1 trillion yen in the quarter, largely in line with consensus.
The quarterly results came after the Tokyo market closed. Shares are down 29% year-to-date.

Espinosa, who has led the company since April 2025, also emphasised progress on a turnaround plan to reduce its global manufacturing footprint and cut its workforce by 15%. About 18 months into the plan, the company has achieved 365 billion yen in savings, Espinosa said.

Chinese university buys Nvidia AI H200 chips despite US ban, records show
text: A Chinese university with ties to the army bought Nvidia’s powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist.

Northwestern Polytechnical University, a member of China’s “Seven Sons of National Defense” group of elite defence-focused universities, bought two H200 chips last month for 874,700 yuan ($123,000), according to an October 21 procurement record on its website, the Reuters news agency reports.
The chips were bought for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record showed.

The Reuters investigation comes as Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang face mounting scrutiny in Washington, DC, over his lobbying for looser ⁠⁠restrictions on sales of AI chips to China, following reports alleging he was targeted by a Chinese spying operation.

The H200 is among Nvidia’s most capable chips for training and running advanced AI systems and is subject to US export licence approvals, which are normally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical.

Northwestern Polytechnical also bought access this year to H200 ‌‌chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five contracts for rented computing capacity from Chinese companies, procurement records show.
Nvidia CEO Huang has argued that continued US sales to China would preserve US technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on its technology.
However, some US lawmakers say access to Nvidia’s most powerful AI chips can speed China’s development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation.
Based in the northwestern city of Xi’an, Northwestern Polytechnical conducts research related to military aircraft, missiles and satellites.

Washington’s Department of Commerce added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over the institute’s alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities, and its military research. Washington tightened the restrictions in 2019, making licences for exporting controlled US technology to the university subject to a policy of denial in most circumstances.

Northwestern Polytechnical’s purchases show how Chinese institutions with military ties continue to obtain US AI computing power through domestic suppliers, either by buying chips outright or renting access to servers containing them.

A Reuters review of 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services ⁠⁠that use such chips through domestic suppliers.
Several had close links to China’s defence industry or military research.

US President Donald Trump’s administration began allowing some H200 exports to China on a case-by-case basis in January. But that policy did not lift the separate restrictions applying to Entity List organisations such as Northwestern Polytechnical.

Both Democrats and Republicans in the US Congress have urged stronger controls on China’s access to advanced AI ⁠⁠chips, such as chip-tracking requirements, and greater congressional oversight of exports.
